## Description

Measure net equity issuance by tracking changes in shares outstanding over a multi-year formation window, with adjustments for splits, stock dividends, mergers, and other share-count changes. Rank eligible stocks from low to high net issuance and test a diversified long-only portfolio tilted toward low-issuance firms; a long-short research variant may be evaluated separately if borrow and shorting constraints are modeled.

## Where it may fit

Long-horizon cross-sectional equity selection; not intended as a standalone hedge in bear markets or during broad factor crashes.

## Vehicles

Common stocks; long-only diversified stock portfolio or factor research portfolio.

## Required data

Point-in-time shares outstanding, split-adjusted prices, issuance/repurchase and corporate-action history, market capitalization, delisting returns, industry classification, and realistic cost estimates.

## Caveats

The cited study discusses the net-stock-issues anomaly among several equity anomalies, but does not validate every formation window or portfolio rule. Corporate actions and share-count data can be messy; define how acquisitions, spin-offs, ADRs, and missing share counts are handled. Test incremental value against existing buyback/shareholder-yield and value factors.

## References

- <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1540-6261.2008.01371.x>

## Source confidence

- **Description basis:** Research-informed factor definition with a reasonably clear operational path; medium confidence in the historical anomaly rationale, low confidence in future net returns of this implementation. Not backtested here.
- **Reference review:** Research reference added; candidate not independently backtested. — Fama and French (2008), “Dissecting Anomalies,” reports that net-stock-issue returns were pervasive in cross-sectional regressions and sorts. The paper is evidence for the anomaly, not a guarantee of a tradable future premium.
- **Metadata alignment:** New candidate; signal can be specified using multi-year share-count changes, but corporate-action treatment and the formation window must be operationally defined.
